title: 08. Multi-Agent & Patterns: CHUNKING STRATEGIES (Part 1 of 3)
summary: Chunking is how you split documents into pieces before embedding and storing in a vector DB. It is the foundation of RAG quality — the WRONG chunk size or strategy can make retrieval fail even with perfect queries.

sections.title: What Is Chunking?
sections.body: > **Chunking is how you split documents into pieces before embedding and storing in a vector DB. It is the foundation of RAG quality — the WRONG chunk size or strategy can make retrieval fail even with perfect queries.**

sections.title: Why Chunking Is Critical
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              WHY CHUNKING MATTERS SO MUCH                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  CHUNKING PROBLEM 1: TOO LARGE
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Chunk size: entire document (5000 words)

  Chunk content:
  "Chapter 1: Introduction to Python...
   Chapter 2: Variables and Types...
   Chapter 3: Functions...
   Chapter 4: Memory Management [the actual answer]...
   Chapter 5: Concurrency..."

  Query: "Python memory management"
  Embedding: Average of ALL 5000 words → diluted signal!
  The memory management content is "buried" in the embedding.
  Search might MISS this chunk entirely. ❌

  CHUNKING PROBLEM 2: TOO SMALL
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Chunk size: 1 sentence (15 words)

  Chunk content: "Reference counting decrements when objects die."

  Query: "How does Python prevent memory leaks?"
  This sentence IS relevant but has NO context.
  LLM can't generate a good answer from 15 words. ❌

  CHUNKING PROBLEM 3: BREAKING CONTEXT
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Splitting at fixed 500-character boundaries:

  Chunk A: "...The most common cause of memory leaks in Python is
            circular references. This happens when object A holds
            a reference to object B, and object B holds a refer"

  Chunk B: "ence back to object A. Neither can be garbage collected
            because their reference count never reaches zero..."

  Chunk A is INCOMPLETE — ends mid-sentence! ❌
  If only Chunk A is retrieved: answer is incomplete.

  THE GOLDILOCKS PRINCIPLE:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Too small:  Missing context. LLM can't answer.
  Too large:  Diluted embedding. Won't be retrieved.
  Just right: Contains exactly one coherent concept. ✅

  Typical sweet spots by content type:
  ┌────────────────────┬─────────────────┬─────────────────┐
  │  Content Type      │  Chunk Size     │  Strategy       │
  ├────────────────────┼─────────────────┼─────────────────┤
  │  Technical docs    │  512-1024 tokens│  Recursive      │
  │  FAQs/QA pairs     │  128-256 tokens │  Semantic       │
  │  Legal/contracts   │  256-512 tokens │  Sentence       │
  │  Code files        │  Function-level │  Code-aware     │
  │  Books/articles    │  512-1024 tokens│  Hierarchical   │
  │  Chat transcripts  │  Turn-based     │  Contextual     │
  └────────────────────┴─────────────────┴─────────────────┘
```

sections.title: Strategy 1 — Fixed-Size Chunking
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               STRATEGY 1: FIXED-SIZE CHUNKING                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  HOW IT WORKS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Split every N characters (or tokens), add K-character overlap.

  Document: "Python uses reference counting. This means every
             object tracks how many references point to it.
             When the count reaches zero, the object is freed."

  chunk_size=50, overlap=10:
  Chunk 1: "Python uses reference counting. This means every"
  Chunk 2: "every object tracks how many references point to"  ← overlap!
  Chunk 3: "to it. When the count reaches zero, the object"    ← overlap!
  Chunk 4: "object is freed."

  WHY OVERLAP?
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Without overlap:
  Chunk 1: "...When the count reaches zero, the"
  Chunk 2: "object is freed immediately."
  These are about the SAME concept but split across chunks!
  Neither chunk alone is useful. ❌

  With overlap:
  Chunk 1: "...When the count reaches zero, the"
  Chunk 2: "reaches zero, the object is freed immediately."  ← shared!
  Chunk 2 alone makes sense. ✅

  TYPICAL PARAMETERS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  chunk_size:  256-1024 tokens   (depends on content)
  overlap:     10-20% of chunk   (e.g., 50 tokens for 512 chunk)

  PROS:                          CONS:
  ─────────────────────          ────────────────────────────
  ✅ Simple to implement         ❌ Breaks mid-sentence
  ✅ Predictable sizes           ❌ No semantic awareness
  ✅ Fast processing             ❌ Splits coherent paragraphs
  ✅ Good starting point         ❌ Context loss at boundaries
```

sections.title: Strategy 2 — Recursive Character Chunking
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           STRATEGY 2: RECURSIVE CHARACTER CHUNKING              │
│           (The Most Common Production Strategy)                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  HOW IT WORKS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Try to split at NATURAL BOUNDARIES first.
  If chunks still too large → split at next smaller boundary.

  SEPARATOR HIERARCHY (try in order):
  1. "\n\n"  (paragraph breaks)    ← most natural
  2. "\n"    (line breaks)
  3. ". "    (sentence ends)
  4. ", "    (clause breaks)
  5. " "     (word boundaries)
  6. ""      (character — last resort)

  EXAMPLE:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Document:
  "Python Memory Management\n\n
   Python uses reference counting. Every object tracks
   references. When count hits zero, object is freed.\n\n
   Garbage Collection\n\n
   Python also has a cyclic garbage collector for circular
   references that reference counting cannot handle."

  chunk_size=100, overlap=20:

  Step 1: Try split by "\n\n" (paragraph)
  → Chunk A = "Python Memory Management\nPython uses reference
               counting. Every object..."         (85 chars) ✅ fits
  → Chunk B = "Garbage Collection\nPython also has a cyclic..."
                                                  (90 chars) ✅ fits

  WHY THIS IS BETTER THAN FIXED SIZE:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Fixed Size:                     Recursive:
  ─────────────────────────       ─────────────────────────────
  "...reference counting.         "Python uses reference counting.
   Every object tracks            Every object tracks references.
   references. When count"        When count hits zero, object
  ← cuts mid-concept!             is freed."
                                  ← complete, self-contained ✅

  BEST FOR: 80% of use cases. Start here.
```

sections.title: Strategy 3 — Semantic Chunking
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               STRATEGY 3: SEMANTIC CHUNKING                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  HOW IT WORKS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Detect where the TOPIC CHANGES by measuring embedding similarity
  between consecutive sentences.

  Step 1: Split into sentences
  Step 2: Embed each sentence
  Step 3: Compute similarity between consecutive sentences
  Step 4: Where similarity DROPS → topic boundary → new chunk!

  VISUAL:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  S1: "Python uses reference counting."      embed → v1
  S2: "Each object tracks its own count."    embed → v2  sim(v1,v2)=0.92
  S3: "When count reaches zero, free it."    embed → v3  sim(v2,v3)=0.89
  S4: "The GIL prevents true parallelism."   embed → v4  sim(v3,v4)=0.41 ← DROP!
  S5: "Threads share the same interpreter."  embed → v5  sim(v4,v5)=0.88
  S6: "Use multiprocessing for CPU tasks."   embed → v6  sim(v5,v6)=0.85

  Similarity drops at S3→S4 (0.89 → 0.41):
  CHUNK 1: S1 + S2 + S3 (reference counting topic)
  CHUNK 2: S4 + S5 + S6 (GIL/parallelism topic)

  WHY THIS IS POWERFUL:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Fixed/Recursive:                Semantic:
  ─────────────────────────       ─────────────────────────────
  Chunks by SIZE                  Chunks by MEANING
  May mix multiple topics         Each chunk = one coherent topic
  Arbitrary boundaries            Natural topic boundaries
  Query embeds to chunk           Query topic maps to chunk topic
                                  dramatically better retrieval ✅

  THRESHOLD TUNING:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  similarity_threshold = 0.5:  Very fine-grained (many small chunks)
  similarity_threshold = 0.7:  Balanced (recommended)
  similarity_threshold = 0.9:  Coarse-grained (few large chunks)

  COST:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Need to embed EVERY SENTENCE at indexing time.
  For 1M sentences × $0.0001/embed = $100 in embeddings.
  Worth it for high-quality knowledge bases.
```

sections.title: Strategy 4 — Sentence Window Chunking
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               STRATEGY 4: SENTENCE WINDOW CHUNKING             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  HOW IT WORKS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Index: small, precise units (1 sentence)
  Retrieve: surrounding context window (±N sentences)

  This separates INDEXING (precision) from RETRIEVAL (context).

  DOCUMENT SENTENCES:
  S1: "Python manages memory automatically."
  S2: "It uses reference counting as primary mechanism."
  S3: "When an object's count hits zero, it's freed."       ← INDEXED
  S4: "Cyclic garbage collection handles circular refs."
  S5: "The gc module provides manual control."

  Query: "How does Python free memory?"

  Step 1: SEARCH finds S3 (best match)
  "When an object's count hits zero, it's freed."

  Step 2: RETRIEVE S3 ± 2 sentences (window=2)
  → S1 + S2 + [S3] + S4 + S5  ← full context!

  LLM gets: complete explanation, not just the matching sentence ✅

  WHY IT WORKS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Small index units = precise embedding = accurate retrieval
  Large context window = complete information for LLM

  Best of both worlds!

  WINDOW SIZE GUIDE:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  window=1: ±1 sentence (3 total)   → Dense technical writing
  window=2: ±2 sentences (5 total)  → Standard documentation
  window=3: ±3 sentences (7 total)  → Narrative/explanatory text
```

sections.title: Strategy 5 — Hierarchical Chunking
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               STRATEGY 5: HIERARCHICAL CHUNKING                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  HOW IT WORKS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Store chunks at MULTIPLE granularity levels simultaneously.
  Search at fine level, retrieve at appropriate level.

  DOCUMENT STRUCTURE:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Level 0 (document):   "Python Memory Guide" (entire doc)
       │
       ├── Level 1 (section): "Reference Counting" (500 words)
       │        │
       │        ├── Level 2 (paragraph): "How it works" (100 words)
       │        ├── Level 2 (paragraph): "Pros and cons" (100 words)
       │        └── Level 2 (paragraph): "Code examples" (100 words)
       │
       └── Level 1 (section): "Garbage Collection" (500 words)
                │
                ├── Level 2 (paragraph): "Cyclic GC" (100 words)
                └── Level 2 (paragraph): "gc module" (100 words)

  HOW RETRIEVAL WORKS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Step 1: Search at Level 2 (paragraphs) → most precise
  Step 2: If confidence low → "zoom out" to Level 1 (section)
  Step 3: If still needed → Level 0 (full doc context)

  Specific question: "What is reference counting?"
  → Level 2 paragraph is sufficient ✅

  Broad question: "How does Python memory work overall?"
  → Level 1 section gives better coverage ✅

  WHY HIERARCHICAL?
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Single-level:    One size fits all → often wrong size
  Hierarchical:    Right size for the question depth ✅
  Parent context:  Fine result always linked to parent context
  Summary chains:  Level 1 has summary of Level 2 chunks below it
```

sections.title: Strategy 6 — Code-Aware Chunking
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               STRATEGY 6: CODE-AWARE CHUNKING                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  PROBLEM WITH NAIVE CHUNKING ON CODE:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Fixed-size splitting of code:

  Chunk 1:                           Chunk 2 (split mid-function!):
  "def calculate_embedding(         "    model=EMBED_MODEL,
       text: str,                       )
       model: str = 'ada'              return response.data[0]"
  ) -> list[float]:
      '''Get embedding.'''
      response = client.embed("

  BROKEN! The function is split across two chunks.
  Neither chunk makes sense alone.

  CODE-AWARE CHUNKING:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Use Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) to understand code structure.
  Split at NATURAL CODE BOUNDARIES:

  BOUNDARY 1: Function/Method level
  → Each function = one chunk
  → Includes: docstring + signature + body

  BOUNDARY 2: Class level
  → Small class = one chunk
  → Large class = one chunk per method

  BOUNDARY 3: Module level
  → Group of related functions
  → Imports + utility functions

  EXAMPLE CODE CHUNK (function-level):
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  "def calculate_embedding(
       text: str,
       model: str = 'text-embedding-ada-002'
   ) -> list[float]:
       '''Get embedding vector for text using OpenAI API.
       Args: text (str): Input text to embed
       Returns: list[float]: 1536-dimensional embedding
       '''
       response = client.embeddings.create(
           input=[text], model=model
       )
       return response.data[0].embedding"

  This is a COMPLETE, SELF-CONTAINED unit of code. ✅

  METADATA TO INCLUDE WITH CODE CHUNKS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  {
    "content":    "def calculate_embedding...",
    "type":       "function",
    "name":       "calculate_embedding",
    "file":       "embeddings.py",
    "module":     "utils.embeddings",
    "language":   "python",
    "docstring":  "Get embedding vector for text...",
    "calls":      ["client.embeddings.create"],
    "parameters": ["text: str", "model: str"],
    "returns":    "list[float]",
  }

  Rich metadata → better filtering + search ✅
```

sections.title: Strategy 7 — Proposition Chunking
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               STRATEGY 7: PROPOSITION CHUNKING                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  HOW IT WORKS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Transform each passage into ATOMIC FACTUAL PROPOSITIONS.
  One proposition = one standalone fact.

  Original paragraph:
  "LangChain was created by Harrison Chase in October 2022.
   It became the fastest growing open-source project of 2023,
   reaching 60,000 GitHub stars. It supports Python and
   JavaScript, and integrates with over 50 LLM providers."

  Decomposed into propositions:
  P1: "LangChain was created by Harrison Chase."
  P2: "LangChain was created in October 2022."
  P3: "LangChain reached 60,000 GitHub stars in 2023."
  P4: "LangChain was the fastest growing open-source project of 2023."
  P5: "LangChain supports Python."
  P6: "LangChain supports JavaScript."
  P7: "LangChain integrates with over 50 LLM providers."

  WHY THIS IS POWERFUL:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Query: "When was LangChain created?"
  → P2 DIRECTLY answers this with ONE precise embedding ✅

  vs. embedding the full paragraph:
  → Full paragraph embedding is diluted across ALL facts
  → Might not rank highest for this specific question

  TRADEOFF:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ✅ Maximum precision for factual QA
  ✅ Each chunk is perfectly self-contained
  ❌ High cost: need LLM to decompose ALL documents
  ❌ Loses flowing explanation / narrative context
  ❌ 3-5x more chunks = larger index

  BEST FOR: FAQ systems, factual databases, knowledge bases
  NOT FOR: Explanatory docs, tutorials, how-to guides
```
